big_idea: The same pattern rule can be shown with different things — animals, sounds, movements, shapes, or letters — and it is still the same rule.
learning_intention: We are learning to translate one pattern rule into different representations and prove that the rule stays the same.
student_learning_goal: I can take one rule and show it as a parade of animals, sounds, and movements.
success_criteria: I can take an animal parade and show its rule as a sound parade.
I can take a sound parade and show its rule as a body-movement parade.
I can tell my partner what stayed the same (the rule) and what changed (the things).
lesson_specific_materials: Anchor chart from previous lessons (PATTERN, CORE, RULE already up)
Three pre-built parade strips for the opening reveal: one animal ABB (Bea-Finn-Finn), one sound ABB (clap-stomp-stomp using M3 cards), one body ABB (tall-small-small with photo cards or improvised)
Sound and Movement Cards (M3) — full set on the carpet, plus 5 sets for partner translation
Sticky notes pre-written with rule labels (AB, ABB, AAB, ABC) for the assignment phase
Class formative tracker for Lesson 3 (provided in assessment_suite stage)

minds_on.hook: Coco built three parades that look totally different — but he says they all follow the SAME rule. Are we sure?
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet. Lay all three pre-built strips in a line on the floor: animal ABB, sound ABB, body ABB.

Say to students: 'Friends, Coco has a puzzle. He showed me three parades — one is animals, one is sounds, one is bodies. Coco says all three have the SAME rule. Look at them. Do you believe Coco?' Take responses. (Most will say no — they look different.)

'Today we are going to PROVE Coco right or wrong by finding the rule of each one. If the rules match, Coco wins. If they do not, Coco owes us cookies.' Smile.

'Yesterday we learned that every pattern has a RULE we name with letters. Today we add a new word — TRANSLATE. When we take one rule and show it a different way, that is translating. We are going to translate animals into sounds and bodies. Watch me first, then you and your partner will do it.'
student_actions: Sit in a circle on the carpet, facing the three parade strips.
Predict whether the three parades follow the same rule or different rules.
Listen and watch as the teacher leads the reveal.
Repeat the new word 'translate' aloud as a class.

steps.instruction: Whole group: see the expanded walkthrough below. The opening reveal of the three same-rule parades is fully scripted there. After the reveal, leave all three strips, their loops, and the rule sticky (ABB) in view as a reference for partner work.
steps.teacher_prompt: Follow the expanded_walkthrough section verbatim. Leave the three strips and the rule sticky in view as anchors during partner work.

steps.instruction: Hand each pair a pre-built animal strip showing one rule (assign by readiness — AB, ABB, AAB, or ABC). Their job is to translate the same rule into TWO new versions: a sound version using Sound and Movement Cards (M3), and a body-movement version (no cards — they invent it). They write the rule on a sticky and place it next to all three.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'You and your partner just got an animal parade. Find its rule and write it on a sticky. Then translate the SAME rule into TWO more parades — one with sound cards, one with your bodies. The rule has to stay the same. Only the things change. When you finish, tap your partner and say: "Same rule?" and show all three.'

steps.instruction: Circulate. Each pair must show all three versions before they finish. Ask each child individually: 'What stayed the same in all three?' (the rule) and 'What changed?' (the things). Record on the formative tracker. Look especially for the language 'the rule' or 'the letters' — that is the abstraction marker.
steps.teacher_prompt: Stop at each pair. Ask one child to read all three versions: animal, sound, body. Then: 'What stayed the same?' Listen for: 'the rule' / 'ABB' / 'the letters'. Then: 'What changed?' Listen for: 'the animals' / 'the sounds' / 'the bodies'. Record on the tracker.

steps.instruction: Optional extension for early-finishing pairs: swap the rule sticky with another pair. Now they have a new rule to translate into three forms — animal, sound, body. This forces them to BUILD from the rule rather than READ from a parade.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to extending pairs: 'Trade rules with another pair. Now you only have a sticky — you do not have a parade. Build all THREE parades from just the rule. Animal, sound, body. Same rule.'

differentiation.for_emerging: Stay with AB rules only. Pre-place the first cell of the sound version and demonstrate the first body position to give a launchpad. Pair with a confident peer who can model the body version first. Accept verbal translation if writing or placing is too much.
differentiation.for_extending: Use ABB, AAB, or ABC rules. After the three translations, ask: 'Could you show this same rule a FOURTH way? Could you use shapes — circle and square? Or letters from the alphabet?' This previews Grade 2 multi-representation work.
differentiation.for_ell_or_iep: Lean on the body-movement translation as the entry point — it requires no language. Once the child can do tall-small-small or jump-freeze-freeze, scaffold backward to the cards and the rule label. Accept gestures or sounds as proof of understanding. Provide pre-printed letter rule cards (A, B, C) so the child can place letters above each cell to bridge.
differentiation.for_movement_learners: These children often grasp this lesson fastest. Invite them to lead the class through their body version during consolidation, calling out the rule rhythmically as they move ('A-B-B, A-B-B').

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Can the child translate the rule into a second and third version? Can they articulate that the rule stayed the same and only the surface changed? Do they self-correct when their second version drifts off the rule (e.g., ABB becoming ABBB)? Do they use rule language ('ABB') or only describe the things ('clap, stomp, stomp')?
formative_check.how_to_record: Tick the appropriate column on the Lesson 3 formative tracker.
tracker_columns: Names what stayed the same (the rule)

discussion_prompts: Who would like to show their three parades to the class? (Take 2–3 pairs.)
When you watched [pair name]'s three parades, what was the rule? How did you know it was the same?
Could we make this same rule a FOURTH way? What else could we use — shapes? Numbers? Letters from the alphabet?
consolidation.exit_routine: Each child whispers to a partner: 'My rule was ___, and I translated it three ways: with ___, ___, and ___.' Then tidy. Teacher listens for children who name the rule label confidently versus those who only name the things.

assessment_in_this_lesson.evidence_collected: Class formative tracker for C1.2, plus completed student worksheet 'Same Rule, Three Ways'. The standalone 'Same Rule Check' formative is administered AFTER this lesson and BEFORE Lesson 4.
assessment_in_this_lesson.rationale: C1.2 (translation) is the unit's most abstract Grade 1 expectation because it requires children to look past surface features to the underlying rule. The teacher needs evidence of who has crossed that abstraction line before Lesson 4 (justifying predictions and finding missing) requires it implicitly. This lesson's keystone status is reflected in the expanded_walkthrough below.

expanded_walkthrough.title: The Three Parades Reveal — Translating the Rule
expanded_walkthrough.rationale: Grade 1 children naturally read patterns by surface features (the animals, the colours, the sound). C1.2 requires them to abstract past the surface to the underlying RULE. This is the unit's conceptual hinge, and the moment is fragile — many children will say 'no, they are different' the first time. This script walks the teacher through the reveal step by step, including how to recover when the abstraction does not land. The Grade 1 difference from Kindergarten: in K we just named what stayed the same as 'the core'; in Grade 1 we name it as 'the RULE' using letter labels (AB, ABB, etc.). Insist on the rule label.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Three short parade strips, all sharing the SAME ABB rule, laid side by side on the carpet: (1) Bea-Finn-Finn-Bea-Finn-Finn animal version, (2) clap-stomp-stomp-clap-stomp-stomp version using Sound and Movement Cards, (3) tall-small-small-tall-small-small using body-position photo cards or improvised body shapes. A Core Loop Frame ready in the teacher's hand. A blank sticky note ready to write the rule label. Coco the puppet visible. Anchor chart with PATTERN, CORE, RULE already taped on.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Hold up Coco. Say to students: 'Coco showed me three parades today, and Coco swears they have the SAME rule. Let's see if we can prove it.'

Point to Strip 1 (animals). 'Read this parade with me.' Lead the class: 'Bea, Finn, Finn, Bea, Finn, Finn.' Place the loop around the first Bea-Finn-Finn group. 'And what is the core here?' (Bea-Finn-Finn.) 'And the rule?' Wait. Let a child say A-B-B. Write 'ABB' on a sticky and place it next to the strip. 'Yes — ABB.'

Point to Strip 2 (clap-stomp-stomp). 'Now this parade — read it with your hands and feet.' Lead the class: clap, stomp, stomp, clap, stomp, stomp. Pick up the loop and place it around the first clap-stomp-stomp group. 'What is the core?' (clap-stomp-stomp.) 'And the rule?' Let a child say A-B-B. 'Same rule!' Write another 'ABB' sticky and place it next to Strip 2.

Point to Strip 3 (tall-small-small). 'And this one — let's do it with our bodies. Stand TALL when I point here, crouch SMALL when I point there.' Lead the class through: tall, small, small, tall, small, small. Loop the first tall-small-small group. 'What is the core?' (tall-small-small.) 'And the rule?' (ABB.) Place the third 'ABB' sticky.

Pause. Step back. Show the three identical 'ABB' stickies in a row. 'Coco said all three parades had the same rule. Look — three stickies, all say ABB. The RULE is the same. Only the THINGS we used are different. Animals, sounds, bodies — but all ABB.'

Pause and let it land. 'When the rule is the same, the pattern is the SAME pattern. That is what TRANSLATE means — same rule, different things. Coco wins. No cookies for us.'

Then the Grade 1 stretch: 'Quick — partner talk. If I made a FOURTH parade with the same rule but used shapes instead — circle, square, square, circle, square, square — would that still be ABB?' (Yes.) 'And if I used numbers — 1, 2, 2, 1, 2, 2 — same rule?' (Yes.) 'The rule does not care what we use. The rule is the rule.'
expected_student_responses: Several children will insist the parades are different because the things in them are different — this is normal and expected.
Some children will count cells ('they all have six') without seeing ABB structure.
A child may say 'they all go ONE-TWO-TWO, ONE-TWO-TWO' before the teacher names it ABB — validate this and supply the formal label.
A child may immediately recognize ABB and say 'they are all ABB' — invite them to teach the class.
A child may confuse ABB with AAB on the sound version (clap-clap-stomp vs clap-stomp-stomp) — common slip; loop the core slowly to clarify.
common_misconceptions: 'They are different patterns because one has bears and the other has claps.' — surface-feature thinking, the most common Grade 1 response on first exposure.
'It's the same because they have the same number of things.' — confusion between length and rule.
'It's ABB because there are three things.' — confusion between length of the core and its structure (any 3-cell core could be ABB, AAB, or ABC).
Saying 'AB' for an ABB parade — child read the first two cells only and stopped.
recovery_moves: If a child is stuck on surface features: physically slide all three loops on top of each other and ask 'do the loops have the same letters? Same A and same B in the same order?'
If a child confuses length and rule: lay out an 8-cell animal parade and a 4-cell clap-stomp parade with the same AB core. Ask 'is the rule the same?' Lead them to see length is independent of rule.
If a child says ABB for any 3-cell pattern: take an AAB pattern (Bea-Bea-Finn) and ask 'is this ABB?' Walk through pointing letter by letter: 'A-A-B. Two As, then a B. Different rule.'

If a child names the structure in their own words: validate first, then supply the formal language. 'Yes — you said ONE-TWO-TWO, ONE-TWO-TWO. Mathematicians call that an ABB rule. Same idea, just letters.'

worksheet_brief.purpose: Independent practice of C1.2 — translating one given pattern rule into two additional representations.

parts_outline.task: Show an animal ABB pattern (Bea-Finn-Finn-Bea-Finn-Finn) at the top of the page with the rule label 'ABB' visible. Below it, two empty parade strips. Student fills the first with sound icons (clap/stomp) and the second with body icons (tall/small) — same ABB rule.

Show three small parade rows side by side: one animal, one sound, one body. Two follow the same rule (AAB), one is different (ABB). Student circles the two that match AND writes the rule (AAB) on a line.

Empty three-row template with a rule bank (AB, ABB, AAB, ABC). Student picks a rule, writes it on the line, and fills all three rows: animal, sound, body. Bottom of page: 'My rule was ___' with a small writing line.
